intro: In this college you'll learn how to talk about your free time outside the home: becoming a member of a club, doing a sport or hobby, giving your opinion about exercise, and describing how people look.

paragraphs.heading: Welcome — life outside the house
paragraphs.text: Welcome to theme fifteen. Its title is [[Buiten de deur]], which means 'out of the house' — literally 'outside the door'. This theme is all about your free time, which in Dutch is [[de vrije tijd]]. In the Netherlands, life really does happen outside the door: people cycle, they swim, they join clubs, and they love to chat about it afterwards. So this is a wonderful theme for making friends and feeling at home. The most useful word here is [[de hobby]], your hobby, and the word [[de sport]], sport. When someone asks about your free time, you will hear [[Wat doe je in je vrije tijd?]], meaning 'what do you do in your free time?'. A friendly, simple answer is [[In mijn vrije tijd doe ik aan sport.]], 'in my free time I do sport'. Another lovely word to know is [[de uitdaging]], which means 'the challenge' — Dutch people often describe a new hobby as a nice challenge. As always, I explain everything in English, but every Dutch word is spoken by a native voice, so repeat each phrase out loud after me. Let's open the door together. [[Laten we beginnen!]]

paragraphs.heading: Becoming a member: lid worden
paragraphs.text: A big part of Dutch life is joining a club, which is called [[de vereniging]], an association. There are clubs for everything: football, swimming, music, you name it. To say 'I want to become a member', you say [[Ik wil lid worden van de sportschool.]], 'I want to become a member of the gym'. That little phrase [[lid worden]] means 'to become a member', and a member is [[het lid]]. The place where you exercise is [[de sportschool]], the gym. Before you start, there is almost always paperwork. You may have to register, so listen for [[Moet ik me van tevoren inschrijven?]], 'do I have to register in advance?'. The verb [[inschrijven]] means 'to sign up'. Every club costs money, and that monthly fee has a special word: [[de contributie]]. A very practical question is [[Hoeveel kost de contributie per maand?]], 'how much is the membership fee per month?'. Here is a warm cultural tip: Dutch clubs are run mostly by volunteers, and members are expected to help out a little too — making coffee, or doing a turn at the bar. That spirit of pitching in is a real key to belonging, so when someone asks for help, a cheerful 'yes' goes a long way.

paragraphs.heading: What you must — and need not — do
paragraphs.text: Now a small but powerful piece of grammar. The word [[moeten]] means 'must' or 'have to'. For example, at a club you might hear [[Je moet je eerst inschrijven.]], 'you have to register first'. But how do you say something is NOT necessary? Here is the trick that surprises every learner: in Dutch you do not say 'moeten niet'. Instead you use [[hoeven niet te]] plus a verb. So [[Je hoeft geen lid te worden om mee te doen.]] means 'you don't have to become a member to join in'. And [[Je hoeft niet elke dag te sporten.]] means 'you don't have to do sport every day'. Notice that little word [[te]] sitting before the verb at the end — that is the signal of 'hoeven'. Be careful, though: 'need not' is [[hoeven niet te]], but 'must not' is something different, like [[Je mag hier niet roken.]], 'you may not smoke here'. So 'don't have to' and 'mustn't' are two very different ideas in Dutch — do not mix them up! Practise this pair out loud: [[Ik moet betalen]], 'I have to pay', and [[Ik hoef niet te betalen]], 'I don't have to pay'. Once this clicks, you sound much more natural.

paragraphs.heading: Liking it and keeping it up
paragraphs.text: Let's talk about what you enjoy. There are two warm ways to say it. First, [[houden van]] means 'to like' or 'to love' something in general. For example, [[Ik houd van zwemmen en fietsen.]], 'I like swimming and cycling'. You can also say [[hou]] instead of [[houd]] — both are fine. Second, [[zin hebben in]] means 'to feel like' something right now. So [[Heb je zin in een wedstrijd?]] means 'do you feel like a match?' — and [[de wedstrijd]] is the match. With a verb you say it like this: [[Heb je zin om mee te gaan?]], 'do you feel like coming along?'. Hobbies are easy to talk about: [[Wat is jouw hobby?]], 'what is your hobby?', and a calm answer is [[Ik houd van lezen en wandelen.]], 'I like reading and walking'. The real secret to any hobby, though, is to keep it up — in Dutch, [[volhouden]]. The training sessions are called [[de training]], and your teammates are [[het team]]. A lovely Dutch saying captures the idea perfectly: [[Oefening baart kunst.]], literally 'practice gives birth to skill' — in other words, practice makes perfect. So be patient with yourself and just keep going.

paragraphs.heading: Opinions and describing how people look
paragraphs.text: Dutch people love giving opinions, and the magic phrase is [[Ik vind]], 'I think' or 'I find'. For example, [[Ik vind sport gezond.]], 'I think sport is healthy', or [[Ik vind voetbal saai.]], 'I find football boring'. To ask back, you say [[Wat vind jij van sport?]], 'what do you think of sport?'. There is even a famous saying about exercise: [[Een gezonde geest in een gezond lichaam.]], 'a healthy mind in a healthy body'. Now, describing appearance. To say how someone looks, Dutch uses a verb that wraps around the sentence, as in [[Hij ziet er sportief uit.]], which means 'he looks sporty'. For features you use [[hebben]], 'to have': [[Hij heeft kort, donker haar en een baard.]], 'he has short, dark hair and a beard'. The hair is [[het haar]], a beard is [[de baard]], and glasses are [[de bril]]. A friendly compliment you will hear at the hairdresser or after a holiday is [[Wat is je haar lang!]], 'your hair is so long!'. One small adjective rule: before a 'de'-word the adjective takes an extra -e, so we say [[lang blond haar]] but [[het lange haar]]. Don't worry about getting it perfect — people will understand you anyway.

paragraphs.heading: At the club desk — and well done!
paragraphs.text: Let's put it all together at a gym reception. You walk in and the staff member, [[de medewerker]], says [[Goedemorgen, kan ik u helpen?]], 'good morning, can I help you?'. You answer warmly: [[Ja, ik wil graag lid worden. Wat kost de contributie?]], 'yes, I'd like to become a member; what does the fee cost?'. Maybe they offer something nice: [[U mag eerst gratis een proefles doen.]], 'you may first do a free trial lesson' — a [[proefles]] is a trial lesson, and [[gratis]] means 'free'. You can ask [[Moet ik me inschrijven?]], 'do I have to register?', and they might reassure you: [[Voor de proefles hoeft u zich niet in te schrijven.]], 'for the trial lesson you don't have to register'. Finish with [[Hoe laat zijn jullie open?]], 'what time are you open?'. Two cheerful little phrases will make you sound like a local: [[Doe je mee?]], 'are you joining in?', and [[Veel plezier met sporten!]], 'have fun doing sport!'. So this week, be brave: walk through a door, ask one question, and join in. That is exactly how you build a life here. [[Heel goed gedaan!]] Well done — I'll see you in the next theme!
